6.2. Classical Heat Flow🔗

The heat operator, Gaussian kernel, initial convolution, Duhamel formula, and comparison principles form one continuous construction. On bounded domains, energy identities give backward uniqueness, and a localization argument shows that every classical solution is smooth in the interior.

6.2.1. The Heat Operator and Classical Problems🔗

The classical heat equation couples a first time derivative to a second spatial derivative. This asymmetry determines the geometry of the problem: time has a preferred direction, initial data live on the time-zero face, and the spatial Laplacian acts on each fixed-time slice. Coordinate zero is time throughout.

The declarations here state equations and initial traces. Explicit whole-space solutions come from the Gaussian kernel and Duhamel's formula, and the variational theory replaces pointwise derivatives by Bochner-space identities on bounded domains.

Theorem 6.2

✓L∃∀N

With coordinate zero reserved for time, the classical heat operator on \mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n is

Hu=\partial_tu-\Delta_xu.

HeatEquation.heatOperator is an ordinary function on Euclidean spacetime. It computes the time-coordinate partial derivative and the Laplacian of the fixed-time spatial slice. Like Mathlib's Fréchet derivative, it is defined for every u, and the analytic theorems state the regularity they need.

Theorem 6.5
Loading preview

✓L∃∀N

Suppose u and v are differentiable at z=(t,x) and their fixed-time spatial slices are C^2 at x. Then the heat operator preserves their sum at z. It also commutes with multiplication by a real constant:

H(u+v)=Hu+Hv,\qquad H(cu)=c\,Hu.

The scalar identity holds without regularity assumptions on u, using the total derivative operators. These two calculus lemmas supply the superposition results for the homogeneous, forced, and initial-value problems.

Proof for Theorem 6.2
uses 0

Expand H=\partial_t-\Delta_x. For a sum, apply the pointwise sum rules to the time derivative and to the Laplacian of the fixed-time spatial slices, then collect terms. For a scalar multiple, pull the constant through both operators and distribute it across the difference.

On a spacetime set U, the homogeneous and forced residual problems are

Hu=0\quad\text{and}\quad Hu=f\qquad\text{on }U.

They are represented by PDEProblem values so that explicit formulas and symbolic calculations can target the same ordinary Lean proposition. The problem values contain only equations and domains; differentiability, existence, uniqueness, and boundary regularity belong to separate theorems.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Satisfaction of either bundled problem is equivalent to its pointwise heat operator identity:

u\models\operatorname{Heat}(f,U) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall z\in U,\ H u(z)=f(z),

with f=0 for the homogeneous problem. The forward and reverse directions are also exposed as projection and constructor theorems.

Proof for Theorem 6.4
uses 0

Unfold satisfaction of the bundled PDEProblem. Its equation field is defined pointwise as Hu(z)=f(z) on the stored domain U, so a witness of satisfaction immediately projects to the displayed identity. Conversely, the pointwise identity fills the sole equation field of the problem witness. The homogeneous statement is the specialization f=0.

Through that equivalence, linearity of H becomes closure of the solution sets.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Constant functions solve the homogeneous equation. Under the regularity assumptions of Theorem 6.2 at every point of U, sums, differences, and real linear combinations of homogeneous solutions are again solutions. More generally, if H u=f and H v=g, then H(au+bv)=af+bg. Multiplication of a solution by a constant needs no additional regularity.

    Linear combinations for the nonhomogeneous heat equation.

    Solutions for forcings f and g combine to a solution for a f + b g (Evans's linearity principle).

Proof for Theorem 6.5
uses 1

Apply the pointwise linearity of the heat operator and then substitute the residual equations for the two solutions. The homogeneous results are the zero-forcing specializations.

Cauchy data add a condition on the time-zero slice.

The homogeneous and forced residual problems combine the positive-time equation with an assigned value on the time-zero hyperplane:

Hu=0\ \text{or}\ f\quad(t>0),\qquad u(0,x)=g(x).

The second clause is an equality on the time-zero slice. Continuity up to time zero and convergence of a representation formula to g are separate analytic conclusions, proved for the kernel and Duhamel solutions.

    The equation u_t - Δu = f holds on {t > 0} and u(0,x) = g(x) holds on {t = 0}. Nothing links the two: there is no continuity at t = 0 and no convergence to g as t ↓ 0.

Each bundled problem is equivalent to the conjunction of its heat-operator identity at positive times and its assigned time-zero value:

u\models\operatorname{HeatResidualAssigned}(f,g) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(\forall t>0,\ \forall x,\ Hu(t,x)=f(t,x)\bigr) \ \land\ \bigl(\forall x,\ u(0,x)=g(x)\bigr).

Proof for Theorem 6.7
uses 0

Unfold the bundled initial-value problem. Satisfaction consists of exactly two fields: satisfaction of the positive-time heat problem and satisfaction of the time-zero initial condition. Apply the heat-problem characterization to the first field and unfold the second to obtain the conjunction. Conversely, the two conjuncts construct those two fields and hence the bundled IVP witness.

For sums and general linear combinations of Cauchy problems, the differentiability and spatial C^2 assumptions are needed only on the half-space t>0, where the residual lives.

Superposition also preserves the Cauchy data. If u and v have source terms f,g and initial values u_0,v_0, then au+bv has source af+bg and initial value au_0+bv_0. The theorem family includes the homogeneous and forced equations, with addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, and general real linear combinations.

6.2.2. The Gaussian Heat Kernel🔗

6.2.2.1. The Gaussian Kernel🔗

The Gaussian heat kernel is the canonical positive, mass-one solution used to construct heat flows on Euclidean space. Under the usual regularity and growth hypotheses, convolution with this kernel produces the corresponding heat evolution, and uniqueness theorems identify that evolution with the prescribed solution. Its exponential decay drives positive-time smoothing, while preservation of unit mass expresses conservation of total heat.

The decreasing peak and increasing width must be read together: the total mass stays one as the profile spreads. Verifying the differential equation at positive time is a separate step from proving the mass normalization or the initial limit. The planar Gaussian CAS example handles the first step by the same differentiation and cancellation used for the polynomial and sine heat solutions. Positive time supplies its denominator conditions; the kernel estimates supply the integral information.

Convolution with the heat kernel evolves initial data, much as convolution with a fundamental solution of the Laplacian solves a stationary Poisson problem. Evans (2010, pp. 44–59) develops the kernel and its convolution consequences under explicit analytic hypotheses.

6.2.2.1.1. Example: Verifying the Heat Equation🔗

For n=1 and t>0, the kernel is

\Gamma_1(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi t}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{4t}\right).

To verify \partial_t\Gamma_1=\partial_{xx}\Gamma_1 by hand, compute each side. Write \Gamma_1=C t^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(4t)} with C=(4\pi)^{-1/2}. Then

\partial_t\Gamma_1 =\Gamma_1\!\left(-\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{x^2}{4t^2}\right),

\partial_x\Gamma_1 =\Gamma_1\!\left(-\frac{x}{2t}\right),

\partial_{xx}\Gamma_1 =\Gamma_1\!\left(\frac{x^2}{4t^2}-\frac{1}{2t}\right).

The two expressions coincide term by term. Heat scaling determines the quadratic exponent -x^2/(4t) and the mass-preserving prefactor; their time and spatial derivatives then cancel in exactly the displayed combination.

Physically, the spreading width \sigma(t)=\sqrt{2t} grows as the square root of time. This is the diffusive scaling: doubling the observation time increases the spread by a factor of \sqrt2, not 2. Strict positivity of the Gaussian makes the solution from nonnegative, nonzero continuous data positive everywhere at every positive time (Theorem 6.22), while the influence at distance L\gg\sigma(t) is exponentially small in L^2/t. This gives the parabolic equation infinite propagation speed with exponentially small far-field influence.

Proof for Theorem 6.10
uses 0

Differentiate the Gaussian time factor and exponential factor, compute each spatial second derivative, and sum the diagonal Hessian entries. Both sides reduce to (\lVert x\rVert^2/(4t^2)-n/(2t))\Gamma_n(x,t).

The differential identity verifies the Gaussian formula but does not fix its multiplicative constant: every constant multiple also solves the heat equation. The prefactor is chosen so that the spatial integral equals one, and it is this normalization, not the equation, that the convolution estimates for the initial-value problem depend on.

For a pole (x,t) and radius parameter r>0, the backward heat ball is

E(x,t;r)= \left\{(y,s): \Gamma_n(x-y,t-s)>r^{-n}\right\},

and Watson's mean-value weight is

W_{x,t}(y,s)=\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert^2}{(t-s)^2}.

Every point of a positive-radius heat ball lies strictly before its pole in time, so the denominator is nonzero on the integration domain.

Proof for Theorem 6.13
uses 0

Parabolically scale the domain to the unit heat ball and differentiate the weighted integral with respect to the scale. On each backward-time slice, Watson's transport identity converts that derivative into a spatial flux. The boundary flux and both singular endpoint contributions vanish. Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus therefore make the weighted integral constant in scale, and its zero-scale value is 4u(x,t). Scaling back contributes the factor r^n.

For the kernel solution u(\cdot,t)=\Gamma_n(\cdot,t)*g with g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n) and \int g=M, Fubini and unit kernel mass give \int u(\cdot,t)=M for all t>0. This is conservation of total heat. In probability, the kernel is the transition density of Brownian motion with covariance 2tI, whose generator is \Delta. Unit mass says the particle is somewhere with probability one. For broad classes of uniformly parabolic equations, Aronson's estimates instead compare their fundamental solutions above and below with Gaussian profiles under suitable coefficient hypotheses (Aronson (1967)).

6.2.3. Initial Data and Convolution🔗

The Gaussian kernel turns an initial profile into a positive-time heat flow by spatial convolution. Three facts drive the construction: the kernel is nonnegative, it has mass one, and its mass concentrates at the origin as time approaches zero. Positivity and unit mass give the L^\infty estimate; concentration recovers the initial trace.

For positive time the same formula is smoother than the original datum. Differentiating the Gaussian under the integral proves the heat equation even when the initial profile is assumed only bounded and continuous. The argument has four parts: the convolution formula, the domination needed for differentiation, the PDE residual, and the approximate-identity limit at time zero.

  (hg_cont : Continuous g)
  (hg_bound : ∀ (y : ℝ^n), |g y| ≤ M)
  (x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) :
  |HeatEquation.initialValueSolution g x
        t| ≤
    M

    The heat-kernel evolution preserves uniform bounds.

    If the continuous initial datum satisfies |g| ≤ M, then its heat evolution satisfies the same pointwise bound at every time; taking the optimal M, this is the L∞ contraction property of the heat semigroup. For t ≤ 0 this is the bound on g itself. For t > 0, positivity of the Gaussian kernel, its unit mass, and the Bochner integral triangle inequality give

    |Γ_t * g| ≤ Γ_t * |g| ≤ M Γ_t * 1 = M.

    Evans obtains the same bound for solutions with the growth bound (24) from his §2.3.3(a), Theorem 6 (Maximum principle for the Cauchy problem), applied to u and -u. Continuity of g is used only for measurability.

Proof for Theorem 6.15
uses 0

For constant data, pull the constant through the convolution and use unit mass. For bounded data, dominate the absolute value of the integrand by M\Gamma_n, integrate, and again use unit mass.

Boundedness of g and unit mass control the size of the evolution but say nothing about its derivatives. Those come from the kernel alone: for t>0 the time derivative of the Gaussian is dominated near t by an integrable majorant, so differentiation passes through the integral even though the datum is merely bounded and continuous.

Let g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R be continuous with |g(y)|\le M for every y, fix x\in\mathbb R^n, and let t>0. Then the heat-kernel convolution

s\longmapsto\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_n(x-y,s)\,g(y)\,dy

is differentiable at s=t, with derivative

\int_{\mathbb R^n} \left(\frac{\lVert x-y\rVert^2}{4t^2}-\frac{n}{2t}\right) \Gamma_n(x-y,t)\,g(y)\,dy.

The integrand is the pointwise time derivative of the Gaussian multiplied by the datum, so this is the first "differentiate under the integral sign" step of Evans's heat initial-value theorem. The statement concerns the convolution integral itself; the totalized initial-value formula agrees with it near every positive time, which is how Theorem 6.17 inherits this derivative.

Proof for Theorem 6.16
uses 0

Work on the time ball |s-t|<t/2. There the coefficient \lVert z\rVert^2/(4s^2)-n/(2s) is bounded by \lVert z\rVert^2/t^2+n/t, and the Gaussian \Gamma_n(z,s) is bounded by a constant depending on t times \exp(-\lVert z\rVert^2/(6t)). Their product is therefore dominated by a polynomial in \lVert z\rVert times the slower Gaussian \exp(-\lVert z\rVert^2/(12t)), which is integrable, and multiplying by the global bound M for g keeps it integrable. The dominated differentiation theorem for parameter-dependent integrals then moves the time derivative of the Gaussian inside the integral.

The time derivative is one slot of the first- and second-order calculus needed to evaluate Hu. The same Gaussian majorants control the spatial gradient and Hessian, and since the totalized formula agrees with the convolution on a neighbourhood of every positive time, the derivative just computed transfers to the initial-data convolution unchanged.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let g be continuous and globally bounded. At every positive-time point, the heat-kernel convolution is differentiable in time and Fréchet differentiable in space, with both derivatives obtained by differentiating the Gaussian beneath the integral. It is jointly differentiable in (t,x), every first spatial coordinate derivative is itself spatially differentiable, and the spatial Laplacian may be moved through the convolution integral.

These are dominated-differentiation theorems with explicit integrable Gaussian majorants. They give the first- and second-order regularity that the classical heat residual needs. Joint C^\infty smoothness on the positive-time half-space is the joint smoothness theorem.

Proof for Theorem 6.17
uses 1

Work in a positive-time neighbourhood bounded away from zero. Derivatives of the Gaussian are bounded there by a polynomial times a slower Gaussian, which is integrable and remains an admissible majorant after multiplication by the global bound for g. Apply the parameter-dependent integral theorems for the time derivative, spatial derivative, and Hessian slots, and sum the diagonal Hessian slots to obtain the Laplacian formula.

With both derivatives expressed as integrals against the datum, the residual reduces to an identity between integrands. The time derivative of \Gamma_n(x-y,t) and its Laplacian in x agree pointwise by the kernel equation, so their difference integrates to zero against any bounded g.

Differentiate beneath the integral using Gaussian derivative majorants, then integrate the pointwise heat-kernel identity against the bounded datum.

The positive-time residual says nothing about t=0. Combine the positive-time differentiability and residual theorems with the locally uniform initial-trace theorem.

Positivity of the kernel has a qualitative consequence beyond the L^\infty bound. g\geq0,\quad g(x_0)>0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (\Gamma_n(\cdot,t)*g)(x)>0 \quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n,\ t>0.

Continuity gives a ball on which the datum has a uniform positive lower bound. At a fixed positive time the Gaussian has a positive lower bound on that ball, so the convolution has a strictly positive contribution there; the remaining integrand is nonnegative.

6.2.4. Duhamel's Principle🔗

Duhamel's principle treats a forcing term as a continuous superposition of new initial data inserted at every source time. A source slice created at time s evolves for heat age t-s, and integrating those evolutions from s=0 to s=t produces the forced solution.

The formal difficulty is the moving upper endpoint. Differentiating in the observation time in source-time coordinates produces both an interior derivative and the endpoint value f(x,t). In heat-age coordinates the moving endpoint instead contributes the heat evolution at age t of the time-zero source slice. This representation avoids differentiating the singular zero-age Gaussian directly.

For a spacetime source f and t>0, define

u(x,t)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma_n(x-y,t-s)f(y,s)\,dy\,ds.

The Lean function is zero for t\leq0. For 0<s<t, the inner integral is the heat evolution of the source slice f(\cdot,s) at age t-s. Replacing it by the totalized initial-value solution changes only an endpoint of the time integral. Recovery of the zero initial trace as a limit uses the compact-support estimates of Theorem 6.27.

Proof for Theorem 6.24
uses 0

Substitute the heat age r=t-s, so the integrand is the heat evolution at age r of the source slice at time t-r. For fixed positive age, the initial-value convolution theorem permits source-time and spatial differentiation under the spatial integral. Compact spacetime support bounds all source derivatives on one compact set; convolution with the positive unit-mass kernel transfers those bounds uniformly. These estimates provide the domination needed near both the moving endpoint and positive heat ages.

The residual calculation requires Leibniz differentiation and interchange of the time and spatial derivatives with the integrals.

At a fixed positive-time point, the following hypotheses justify the differentiation of Duhamel's integral: assume continuity and boundedness of each interior source slice, the moving-boundary Leibniz formula with endpoint term f(x,t), and passage of both pure spatial derivatives through the source-time integral, together with interval integrability of the resulting second derivatives. Then

\partial_tu-\Delta_xu=f.

The dominated-differentiation theorem assumes that, on a spatial neighbourhood, the slice evolutions are measurable and integrable in source time, and they and their first coordinate derivatives are spatially differentiable for almost every source time. Measurable derivative covectors with locally uniform, integrable norm bounds then justify spatial interchange and give integrability of the resulting second derivatives. For globally C^2, compactly supported sources, Theorem 6.27 verifies these hypotheses and the moving-endpoint calculation.

Proof for Theorem 6.25
uses 1

Apply the homogeneous heat equation to every interior source slice, integrate that identity over source time, and use the supplied Leibniz and derivative-interchange identities. The two integrated Laplacians cancel, leaving exactly the moving-endpoint contribution f(x,t).

The residual theorem uses the ordinary time derivative and the spatial Laplacian of the Duhamel integral separately. Joint Fréchet differentiability in (t,x) is a stronger statement: it identifies the spacetime time-coordinate derivative in the heat operator with the one-variable derivative of the residual.

Proof for Theorem 6.26
uses 0

Write S(r) for heat evolution. For each r>0, the parameterized convolution theorem gives the joint Fréchet derivative of (t,x)\mapsto [S(r)f(t-r)](x). Compact support bounds its operator norm uniformly in heat age, so dominated differentiation applies first on a fixed age interval. Continuity at the moving upper endpoint then permits the moving-interval rule, which adds the covector (h_t,h_x)\mapsto [S(t)f(0)](x)h_t. This proves joint differentiability for t>0 without differentiating the zero-age kernel.

For a globally C^2, compactly supported source, the Leibniz and interchange hypotheses of the analytic core all follow from the source-evolution lemmas.

Use the source-time representation u(t)=\int_0^t S(t-s)f(s)\,ds, where S(r) is heat evolution and S(0) is the identity. 6.2.5. Maximum, Comparison, and Uniqueness🔗

Parabolic equations propagate information forward from the initial face and inward from the spatial boundary. Their natural boundary is therefore not the entire boundary of a spacetime cylinder: the spatial interior of the terminal-time face is excluded, while its lateral boundary points remain. The parabolic boundary encodes this causal geometry.

The maximum principle rules out a new positive maximum in the positive-time interior. A small perturbation by -\varepsilon t makes the differential inequality strict, compactness supplies a maximizer, and the spatial second-derivative test conflicts with the time derivative at that point. Applying the same result to differences yields comparison and uniqueness.

The maximum-principle argument finds a maximizer over the whole closed set and must then be able to exclude it from the region where the differential inequality holds, and that region is \Omega\times(0,T], terminal face included.

    Evans's parabolic boundary: the lateral boundary together with the initial-time face. For T > 0, the terminal-time section consists of frontier Ω × {T}; spatial interior points at time T are excluded.

The operator to which the argument applies need not be the Laplacian. What the second-derivative test uses at a spatial maximum is only that each principal term is a second derivative in a fixed direction. The directions may vary with the point, but they are held fixed while differentiating the spatial slice; no derivatives of the coefficient fields enter.

For a scalar field u(x,t) on a real normed space, finitely many direction fields \sigma_k(x,t), and a drift b(x,t), define

Pu=u_t-\sum_k D_x^2u[\sigma_k,\sigma_k]+D_xu[b].

The potential variant is P_cu=Pu+c(x,t)u(x,t). The definitions impose no sign condition on c; Theorem 6.34 assumes c\geq0.

Writing \sigma_{ki} for coordinate i of direction \sigma_k, the principal matrix has entries A_{ij}=\sum_k\sigma_{ki}\sigma_{kj}. Every symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix has such a factorization. The theorems use only this semidefinite sign.

Let \Omega be nonempty and open with compact closure, and let T>0. Assume u is continuous on the closed cylinder. At every (x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T], assume its spatial slice is C^2 at x, its time slice is differentiable at t, and Pu\leq0. If u\leq M on the parabolic boundary, then u\leq M throughout the closed cylinder.

The time derivative is required at T even at spatial interior points, where terminal boundary data are not prescribed. It is the two-sided derivative on the real line, not a one-sided derivative within [0,T]. The potential variants use the same hypotheses; the heat versions ask for less at the terminal face.

    Evans's §7.1.4(a), Theorem 8(i): weak parabolic maximum principle.

    For a subsolution of uₜ + Lu ≤ 0 with zero zeroth-order coefficient, the upper bound on the parabolic boundary controls the entire closed cylinder. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the coefficient factorization represents an arbitrary symmetric positive-semidefinite principal matrix.

Proof for Theorem 6.33
uses 0

For \varepsilon>0, the perturbation u_\varepsilon=u-\varepsilon t satisfies Pu_\varepsilon<0 and retains the boundary upper bound. If its maximum on the compact cylinder exceeded M, a maximizer would lie in \Omega\times(0,T]. There the spatial gradient vanishes and every directional second derivative is nonpositive. The time derivative is nonnegative, including at t=T, where comparison with earlier times gives the same sign. Thus Pu_\varepsilon\geq0, a contradiction. Let \varepsilon\downarrow0 to recover the bound for u.

A zeroth-order term cu with c\geq0 does not disturb the argument provided the bound M is nonnegative. At a point where u>M\geq0 the term cu is nonnegative, so it only makes the inequality Pu+cu\leq0 harder to satisfy. This is where the sign restriction on M enters.

Proof for Theorem 6.34
uses 0

The same perturbation u_\varepsilon=u-\varepsilon t produces the additional term -c\varepsilon t, which has the favorable sign because c,\varepsilon,t\geq0. At a positive maximum the zeroth-order term is also nonnegative.

Replacing u by -u turns subsolutions into supersolutions and upper bounds into lower bounds. The sign condition on M flips with it: the minimum principle requires M\leq0, precisely so that -M is an admissible upper bound for -u.

Proof for Theorem 6.35
uses 1

Apply the maximum principle with potential to -u and the nonnegative upper bound -M, then negate the resulting inequality.

For the heat operator, c=0 and the principal part is the full Laplacian, so the sign restriction on M disappears. The statement is repeated for the heat operator so that no factorization of the identity matrix has to be supplied when it is invoked. It is also sharper at the top of the cylinder: derivatives and the differential inequality are needed only on the open slab \Omega\times(0,T). Continuity carries the bound from every shorter cylinder up to the terminal face.

Proof for Theorem 6.36
uses 0

At a spatial maximum \Delta u\leq0, while at a positive-time maximum on [0,s] one has u_t\geq0. The perturbation u_\varepsilon=u-\varepsilon t reduces the non-strict case to this strict contradiction on each cylinder \overline\Omega\times[0,s] with s<T, where the hypotheses hold up to the top face. Every point of \Omega\times(0,T) lies in such a cylinder, and the closed cylinder is the closure of this open slab, so continuity gives the bound everywhere.

Negating a supersolution of the heat equation produces a subsolution with the negated bound.

    The dual heat minimum principle, obtained by applying the maximum principle to -u.

Proof for Theorem 6.37
uses 1

Set w=-u. Then w_t-\Delta w=-(u_t-\Delta u)\leq0, while the boundary hypothesis u\geq M becomes w\leq-M. The weak maximum principle gives w\leq-M throughout the cylinder, which is equivalent to u\geq M.

Applied to a difference w=u-v, the maximum principle compares two functions instead of bounding one.

    Parabolic comparison principle.

    If uₜ-Δu ≤ vₜ-Δv in the positive-time interior and u ≤ v on the parabolic boundary, then u ≤ v throughout the closed cylinder. The proof applies the weak maximum principle (Evans's §7.1.4, Theorem 8, with L = -Δ) to u - v.

Proof for Theorem 6.38
uses 1

Set w=u-v. Linearity of the heat operator gives w_t-\Delta w\leq0, and the boundary assumption gives w\leq0 on the parabolic boundary. The weak maximum principle therefore yields w\leq0 on the closed cylinder, which is exactly u\leq v.

Uniqueness is comparison applied twice.

Compactness of \overline\Omega supplies the point where the perturbed solution attains its maximum. On an unbounded domain, behavior at infinity needs a separate argument.

Let \Omega be nonempty and open with compact closure, and T>0. Under the regularity hypotheses of Theorem 6.38, two classical heat solutions with equal residual on \Omega\times(0,T] and equal parabolic boundary data agree throughout the closed cylinder:

Hu=Hv\ \text{ on }\Omega\times(0,T],\qquad u=v\ \text{ on }\partial_pQ \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=v\ \text{ on }\overline Q.

    Classical heat solutions with the same parabolic boundary values and the same heat residual agree throughout the closed cylinder. This is Evans's §2.3.3, Theorem 5.

Proof for Theorem 6.39
uses 1

The two solutions have the same heat residual and the same parabolic boundary data. Comparison first gives u\leq v; exchanging the two solutions gives v\leq u. Pointwise antisymmetry of the real order then gives u=v on the whole closed cylinder.

On all of \mathbb R^n there is no compact cylinder, and uniqueness fails without some control at infinity: Tychonoff's classical example is a nonzero solution with zero initial data that grows faster than any Gaussian. The remedy in Evans (2010) is a growth bound of the form u(x,t)\leq Ae^{a|x|^2}. Any fixed Gaussian rate a is allowed, however large, and the time horizon T is arbitrary.

Theorem6.40

Let T>0 and a\geq0. Let u be continuous on \mathbb R^n\times[0,T], with C^2 spatial slices and differentiable time slices on \mathbb R^n\times(0,T), and suppose u_t-\Delta u=0 there. If u(x,t)\leq Ae^{a|x|^2} for 0<t<T, then

\sup_{\mathbb R^n\times[0,T]}u=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}u(x,0),

with suprema in the extended reals. The same equality holds with [0,T] replaced by (0,T].

    A classical heat subsolution with one-sided Gaussian growth stays below each upper bound of its initial data, for every finite final time.

    Only interior positive times require derivatives and the differential inequality. Continuity supplies the growth bound at both time faces and the terminal comparison. The initial data need only be bounded above by M; no lower bound is assumed.

Proof for Theorem 6.40
uses 1

Only the upper bound needs work, and the extended-real formulation makes the case of initial data unbounded above trivial. So fix M with u(\cdot,0)\leq M. On a short time interval, of length fixed by a, compare u on a large ball with M plus a small multiple of the growing Gaussian (T_1-t)^{-n/2}\exp\bigl(|x-y|^2/4(T_1-t)\bigr). This barrier solves the heat equation, and on the sphere |x-y|=r it outgrows Ae^{a|x|^2} once r is large. The weak maximum principle on the ball gives u(y,t)\leq M plus the small multiple, and letting the multiple tend to zero gives u(y,t)\leq M. The short intervals are then concatenated up to T. The equality with the positive-time supremum uses continuity at t=0.

The growth bound is needed only for 0<t<T, and the equation only at interior times.

    Two classical solutions of the same forced heat equation with the same initial data and possibly different two-sided Gaussian bounds agree on the closed slab. The forcing need not satisfy any additional regularity assumption.

Proof for Theorem 6.41
uses 1

The difference w=u-v solves the homogeneous equation, vanishes at t=0, and satisfies |w|\leq(A_1+A_2)e^{\max(a_1,a_2)|x|^2}. The maximum principle applied to w and to -w gives \sup w\leq0 and \sup(-w)\leq0.

The weak principle says the maximum is attained on the parabolic boundary. It does not rule out an interior maximum as well. The strong principle says that an interior maximum at a positive time t_0 forces the solution to be constant on the whole cylinder below t_0. The statement is only about the past. Boundary values imposed after t_0 can still change the solution there.

The strong principle is proved for a general operator in nondivergence form. The coefficients multiply second derivatives directly and are never differentiated.

✓L∃∀N

For a matrix field a(x,t), a drift b(x,t), and a potential c(x,t),

Lu=u_t-\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}(x,t)\,\partial_i\partial_ju+Du\cdot b+c\,u.

When a_{ij}=\sum_k\sigma_{ki}\sigma_{kj} and the spatial slice is C^2 at the point, this agrees with the factored operator.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let U be open and connected. Let a, b, c be continuous on U\times(0,T], with a symmetric and \sum a_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\geq\theta|\xi|^2 for some \theta>0. Let u be continuous on \overline U\times[0,T], with C^2 spatial slices and differentiable time slices on U\times(0,T). Suppose Lu\leq0 there and u attains its maximum over the closed cylinder at (x_0,t_0) with x_0\in U and 0<t_0\leq T. If c=0, or if c\geq0 and u(x_0,t_0)\geq0, then u\equiv u(x_0,t_0) on \overline U\times[0,t_0]. The minimum versions hold for Lu\geq0, with u(x_0,t_0)\leq0 in the case c\geq0.

Proof for Theorem 6.43
uses 0

Put M=u(x_0,t_0) and v=M-u\geq0. The sign conditions ensure that v is a supersolution. The argument proves that positivity of v moves forward in time. If v(y,s)>0, a small cubic bump centred at y lies below v at time s. Moved along a segment and damped exponentially in time, the bump remains a subsolution: uniform ellipticity and bounds on the continuous coefficients over a compact piece of the cylinder fix the damping rate. Comparison on the moving ball then keeps v>0 at the end of the segment. Any two points of the connected set U are joined by a finite chain of overlapping balls inside U. So if v(y,s)>0 for some s<t_0, then v(x_0,t_0)>0, which is false. Hence v=0 on U\times(0,t_0), and continuity extends this to \overline U\times[0,t_0].

The proof uses only comparison with explicit barriers. It needs neither boundedness of U nor derivatives of the coefficients. It also uses derivatives only strictly before T, so a maximum at t_0=T is covered.

For the heat equation, a is the identity matrix, b=0, c=0, and \theta=1. The strong principle then holds for extrema of either sign.

Let U be open and connected, and let u be continuous on \overline U\times[0,T], with C^2 spatial slices and differentiable time slices on U\times(0,T). If u_t-\Delta u\leq0 and u attains its maximum over the closed cylinder at an interior point (x_0,t_0) with 0<t_0\leq T, then u is constant on \overline U\times[0,t_0]. The same holds for a minimum of a supersolution.

Proof for Theorem 6.44
uses 1

The heat operator equals the matrix operator with coefficients (I,0,0), identically in u. The identity matrix is symmetric with ellipticity constant one, and constant coefficients are continuous.

The heat case also follows from the mean value formula on heat balls (Theorem 6.13), a route specific to the Laplacian.

A consequence is infinite speed of propagation on bounded domains. With zero boundary values, a nonnegative initial temperature that is positive somewhere makes the temperature strictly positive everywhere inside at every positive time.

Theorem 6.37
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

By the weak minimum principle u\geq0 on the closed cylinder. If u(x,t)=0 for some x\in U and t>0, then (x,t) is an interior minimum, and the strong principle makes u identically zero on \overline U\times[0,t]. This contradicts u(y,0)>0.

On the whole line the same fact is visible in the kernel formula (Theorem 6.22), since the Gaussian is positive. On a bounded interval, the figure computes the zero-boundary solution from its sine series.

The Harnack inequality is a quantitative form of the strong principle. It compares a nonnegative solution at an earlier time with the same solution at a later time, uniformly over a compact subregion. The constant depends on the geometry and the coefficients. It is chosen before the solution.

Let U be open, and let V be connected with compact closure \overline V\subseteq U. Let 0<s<t\leq T. Let a, b, c be continuous on U\times(0,T], with a symmetric and uniformly elliptic; c may have either sign. Then there is C>0 with the following property. Let u\geq0 be continuous on U\times(0,T]. Suppose u has continuous spatial first and second derivatives and a continuous time derivative on U\times(0,T), and Lu=0 there. Then

u(x,s)\leq C\,u(y,t)\quad(x,y\in\overline V),\qquad \sup_V u(\cdot,s)\leq C\inf_V u(\cdot,t).

Proof for Theorem 6.46
uses 0

The proof uses the contact-set method of Krylov and Safonov, in the form presented by Imbert and Silvestre. Suppose a supersolution is small at some point at a later time. Slide a family of paraboloids up from below until they first touch the graph at earlier times. At each contact point the spatial Hessian of the solution is bounded below by that of the paraboloid. The supersolution inequality then bounds the Jacobian of the contact map, using only ellipticity and bounds on the trace and the drift. The change of variables formula turns this into a lower bound on the measure of the set where the solution was small earlier. An expanding barrier and an iteration of this growth step give a measure estimate on nested cylinders. The upper side comes from propagating almost-maximal values forward to later balls. Together they give the comparison on small cylinders, and a finite covering of \overline V gives the constant. A potential of either sign is absorbed by adding one spatial variable z and multiplying by an exponential in z. The potential then becomes a drift in z. The contact argument needs a jointly C^2 gradient. The classical hypotheses stated here are reached by averaging forward in time and letting the width tend to zero.

The coefficients are only assumed continuous.

6.2.6. Energy and Smoothing🔗

The maximum principle compares values. A second family of arguments measures the solution in L^2. On a bounded domain with zero lateral values, the energy E(t)=\int_\Omega u(x,t)^2\,dx can only decrease, and the rate at which it decreases is the Dirichlet energy. Differentiating once more and applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality shows that \log E is convex. A convex function that is finite at the start cannot reach -\infty in finite time unless it was -\infty all along, and this is backward uniqueness: a heat solution that vanishes at a later time vanished at every earlier time. The argument follows §2.3.4 of Evans (2010).

Throughout, \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n\geq1, is a bounded open set with a C^1 graph boundary, and u is C^2 up to the boundary of the cylinder \Omega\times(a,b) and continuous on its closure. The boundary regularity is used only for integration by parts in space.

    The derivative of the Dirichlet energy is -2 ∫ (∂ₜu)². The proof uses the mixed second derivatives of u and the vanishing of ∂ₜu on the lateral boundary; no third derivative is required.

Proof for Theorem 6.47
uses 1

Differentiate under the integral and replace u_t by \Delta u. Green's first identity with the zero boundary values turns 2\int_\Omega u\,\Delta u into -2\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2. For the second identity, the time derivative of |\nabla u|^2 is 2\nabla u\cdot\nabla u_t, and integrating by parts gives -2\int_\Omega\Delta u\,u_t, which is -2\int_\Omega u_t^2 by the equation. The boundary term vanishes because u_t=0 on the lateral boundary, which follows from u=0 there for all times. The proof commutes the mixed second derivatives of u; it never differentiates \Delta u in time, so C^2 regularity is enough.

The first identity gives the familiar energy decay. The second shows that the Dirichlet energy decreases as well, so the rate of decay slows down. Log-convexity of the energy makes this precise.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.47, write E(t)=\int_\Omega u^2\,dx. Then E'(t)=-2\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2 and E''(t)=4\int_\Omega u_t^2 satisfy

\Bigl(-2\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx\Bigr)^2 \leq\int_\Omega u^2\,dx\cdot4\int_\Omega u_t^2\,dx, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad (E')^2\leq E\,E''.

    Cauchy-Schwarz for the first and second square-energy derivatives.

Proof for Theorem 6.48
uses 1

By the first energy identity, E'=2\int_\Omega u\,u_t. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives (E')^2\leq4\int_\Omega u^2\int_\Omega u_t^2, and the right side is E\,E'' by the second identity.

Where E>0 the inequality says (\log E)''=(EE''-(E')^2)/E^2\geq0. The quotient -E'/2E=\int|\nabla u|^2/\int u^2 is the frequency of the solution. Log-convexity says the frequency never increases: a solution with its energy in high modes loses them first and settles toward the lowest mode it contains.

Let a<b, and let u and v solve u_t-\Delta u=0=v_t-\Delta v in \Omega\times(a,b). If u=v on \partial\Omega\times[a,b] and u(\cdot,b)=v(\cdot,b) in \Omega, then u=v on \overline\Omega\times[a,b]. In particular a solution with zero lateral values that vanishes at time b vanishes on the whole closed cylinder.

    Zero lateral and terminal values force vanishing on the closed cylinder.

Proof for Theorem 6.49
uses 1

The difference w=u-v satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 6.47 with zero lateral values, so it suffices to treat w. Its energy E is continuous on [a,b], nonnegative, has E''\geq0, satisfies (E')^2\leq EE'', and E(b)=0. For \varepsilon>0 the function \log(E+\varepsilon) is convex, because (E+\varepsilon)E''-(E')^2\geq EE''-(E')^2\geq0. Convexity on [a,b] gives

E(t)+\varepsilon\leq(E(a)+\varepsilon)^{(b-t)/(b-a)}(E(b)+\varepsilon)^{(t-a)/(b-a)},

and letting \varepsilon\to0 gives E(t)=0 for a<t<b. Continuity of w then gives w=0 on each slice and on the closure.

The regularization by \varepsilon avoids a case analysis on the set where E>0, and it is where the sign condition E''\geq0 is used. The statement holds on any interval [a,b] and for every bounded open \Omega with C^1 graph boundary.

Forward uniqueness also follows from energy decay, since E(0)=0 and E'\leq0 force E=0, or from the maximum principle in Theorem 6.39. Backward uniqueness requires a different argument: the forward maximum principle takes data from the parabolic boundary, which excludes the terminal face.

The second theme is smoothing. A solution with only two spatial derivatives and one time derivative is automatically smooth in the interior, and every derivative is controlled by the L^1 norm of the solution on a slightly larger cylinder. This is Theorem 8 and Theorem 9 of Evans's §2.3.3.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be open and T>0. Suppose u is continuous on \Omega\times(0,T], has continuous first and second spatial derivatives there and a continuous time derivative taken within (0,T], and solves u_t-\Delta u=0 on \Omega\times(0,T]. Then u is C^\infty on \Omega\times(0,T]. Near every point of this set, including points with t=T, u agrees with a function that is C^\infty on an open neighborhood of the point.

    A classical heat solution on Ω × (0,T] has a constructed smooth extension on an open neighborhood of each point, including the terminal time. Only the extension, not the given function, is evaluated smoothly beyond T.

Proof for Theorem 6.50

Definition 6.14
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Fix (x_0,t_0) and a cutoff \chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega) equal to 1 near x_0. Restart the clock at a=t_0/2. The product \chi u solves the heat equation with forcing R, which involves \nabla\chi and \Delta\chi and is therefore supported away from x_0. Duhamel's principle represents \chi u on [a,T] as the Gaussian convolution of \chi u(\cdot,a) at age t-a plus the integral in time of the Gaussian convolutions of R(\cdot,s) at age t-s. The first term is smooth because its age is bounded away from zero near t_0. In the second term, the kernel is evaluated only at spatial offsets bounded away from zero, where \Gamma_n(x,t) extended by 0 for t\leq0 is smooth. Hence the second term is smooth in (x,t) near (x_0,t_0), also when t_0=T.

As in Evans, the proof localizes with a cutoff, writes the result as a heat-kernel integral, and integrates by parts to remove \nabla u. It keeps the terminal time: the extension is smooth on an open set around (x_0,T), while u itself is only asserted smooth within \Omega\times(0,T]. No mixed derivative and no second time derivative are assumed.

The parabolic cylinder of radius r ending at (x,t) is C(x,t;r)=\overline B(x,r)\times[t-r^2,t]. Its spatial radius is r and its height is r^2, matching the scaling u(x,t)\mapsto u(\lambda x,\lambda^2t) of the heat equation. That scaling fixes the power of r in the estimate: each spatial derivative costs r^{-1}, each time derivative costs r^{-2}, and the L^1 norm over a cylinder of volume comparable to r^{n+2} costs r^{-n-2}.

For all n,k,l\geq0 there is a constant C=C_{n,k,l}>0 with the following property. Let u satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 6.50 on \Omega\times(0,T], and let r>0 with C(x,t;r)\subset\Omega\times(0,T]. Then u is integrable on C(x,t;r), the norm of the mixed derivative D_x^kD_t^lu attains its maximum on C(x,t;r/2), and

\max_{C(x,t;r/2)}\bigl\|D_x^kD_t^lu\bigr\| \leq\frac{C}{r^{k+2l+n+2}}\int_{C(x,t;r)}|u|\,dy\,ds.

The derivatives are taken within \Omega\times(0,T], so the cylinder may touch the terminal time, and the norm is the operator norm of the k-linear spatial derivative.

    Every mixed derivative of a C²,¹ heat solution obeys the local spacetime L1 estimate on the closed half cylinder, where its norm attains a maximum. Integrability follows from continuity and compact containment. The constant depends only on the dimension and derivative orders; zero dimension and orders are allowed.

Proof for Theorem 6.51
uses 1

By translation and parabolic scaling, it suffices to treat the unit cylinder ending at (0,0). There fixed cutoffs in space and time, equal to 1 near the half cylinder, localize u. The cutoff residual contains \nabla u; integrating by parts in space moves those derivatives onto a single smooth compactly supported kernel that agrees with the Gaussian on the support of the residual. The representation then expresses u near the half cylinder as an integral of u alone against that kernel and its derivatives, and differentiating under the integral bounds D_x^kD_t^lu by a constant times \int|u|. The constant depends only on the kernel, hence only on n, k and l. Scaling back produces the factor r^{-(k+2l+n+2)}. This is Evans's proof, with the fixed kernel as the representation formula.
